title: About
text:
I’m an Honours student in Actuarial Science and Statistics at the University of Manitoba. I’m drawn to the part of actuarial work where a question about risk becomes a model you can test, so I build projects end to end: data, assumptions, code and a clear write-up.
My three featured projects cover life insurance pricing, options pricing and a neural network for mortality rates.

title: Life Insurance Pricing Model
text:
Life insurers must set a premium today for a promise that may not be paid for decades. This project prices life insurance the way an actuary would from experience data. It generates a portfolio of 10,000 synthetic policies, studies the mortality they produce, turns that study into pricing assumptions, solves for the premium, and then tests how profitable the product stays when reality differs from the assumptions.
It covers three products: Term, Whole Life and Deferred Whole Life (a waiting period, then lifetime coverage). The data is synthetic, so no real or personal information is used. Because the true mortality pattern is known in advance, the accuracy of the mortality study can be measured directly.
The work runs through nine phases: pricing fundamentals, database design, synthetic data, a mortality study, assumptions, a pricing engine, profit testing, sensitivity analysis and a Shiny dashboard.

title: Life Insurance Pricing Model
text:
Tools used

R for simulation, the pricing engine, profit testing and charts, with dplyr, ggplot2, DBI, RSQLite and readxl
SQL (SQLite) for the policy, exposure and death tables
Excel for the assumptions workbook, kept separate from the code so any assumption can be changed
Shiny for the pricing dashboard
Git and GitHub for version control

title: Life Insurance Pricing Model
text:
Key results

The mortality study recovered the true pattern
Deaths divided by exposure, by 5-year age band and smoker status, tracks the mortality curve the data was generated from across ages 40 to 95. At age 65 the Nonsmoker rate is 0.696% observed against 0.700% true, and at age 80 the Smoker rate is 9.33% against 9.40%. The smoker-to-nonsmoker ratio stays close to the 2.5 times built into the simulation. At the youngest and oldest ages, exposure is thin and the observed rates become unreliable, which is a known feature of experience studies.



Observed versus true annual mortality rates by age band and smoker status




Profit margins match their targets
Profit testing projects cash flows year by year and checks them against the pricing engine’s premium. Across six test policies, every achieved margin matched its product’s target: 8% for Term, 15% for Whole Life and 12% for Deferred Whole Life. An early version did not reconcile, giving $9.34 against a target of $17.20. The cause was a timing mismatch, and discounting each cash flow with its own timing fixed it.


Each product has a different dominant risk
Sensitivity analysis prices each product once and then stresses the assumptions: mortality ±10%, interest rate ±1 percentage point and expenses ±10%. The table shows each product’s profit margin under the adverse direction of each stress.

title: Life Insurance Pricing Model
text:
Limitations and assumptions

The data is synthetic, so the results show that the method works, not how a real insurer’s mortality behaves.
The “true” mortality pattern is a Gompertz-Makeham curve with parameters from course material. That is an assumption of the model.
Cash flows use expected values rather than a simulation of individual policies, and premiums are level.
Exposure is thin at the oldest ages (95 and above), so observed rates there are volatile. Ages are grouped into 5-year bands.
Sensitivity was run on one representative policy per product, with single shocks (mortality ±10%, interest rate ±1 point, expenses ±10%), not combined stresses.
The dashboard prices at a fixed 5% interest rate and runs locally in RStudio. It is not hosted online.

title: Life Insurance Pricing Model
text:
What I learned

A model can run without errors and still be wrong. Reconciling two independent calculations, the premium solve and the cash flow projection, caught a discounting mistake that neither would have shown alone.
Price once, test many times. Re-solving the premium under each stress answers the wrong question, because sensitivity testing should hold the premium fixed.
Stress tests need checking too. My first mortality stress changed nothing, because the stressed table never reached the calculations. Checking each function in the chain in turn found the gap.
A Shiny interface can sit on top of a verified engine without changing its logic.

title: Options Pricing Engine
text:
A segregated fund guarantee promises the policyholder at least their money back at maturity. That makes it a put option the insurer has sold. This project builds an option pricing engine in R to price that promise. It prices options three independent ways, a binomial tree, the Black-Scholes formula and Monte Carlo simulation, and checks them against each other. It then tests the models on real Tesla option data and applies them to the guarantee: its price, the fair fee, a delta hedge and a tail reserve.
The project ends in a three-tab Shiny app and a written report.

title: Options Pricing Engine
text:
Key results

Three methods that check each other
The tree handles American options, the formula is exact for European ones and gives the Greeks, and simulation handles products that depend on the path, such as Asian and barrier options. For the same European call (stock 100, strike 100, rate 5%, dividend yield 2%, volatility 20%, one year), they agree closely.



Method
European call price




Binomial tree, 500 steps
9.2231


Black-Scholes formula
9.2270


Monte Carlo, control variate
9.2553 (standard error 0.018)



Put-call parity held to rounding error, and every Greek matched a direct nudge calculation. A control variate cut the simulation error by about 59% compared with plain Monte Carlo.


Real Tesla data shows what one volatility cannot capture
I tested the models on Tesla options expiring in January 2027, saved on 2 November 2026. Most quotes were unusable, and put-call parity showed that the downloaded stock price did not match the price the options were quoted at. Implied volatility near the money was about 44%, against historical volatility of 36% (30 days), 51% (90 days) and 45% (about a year). It also formed a smile, from about 55% at the lowest strikes to about 42% at the highest. A single constant volatility cannot match that.



Implied volatility smile for Tesla options expiring 15 January 2027




Pricing the segregated fund guarantee
The guarantee pays the shortfall between the fund and the guaranteed 100 at maturity. For a 10-year policy, with a 3.8% interest rate and 20% volatility, the results per 100 invested are below.



Result
Without mortality and lapses
With mortality and lapses




Cost of the guarantee
13.77
8.08


CTE95 reserve per 100 sold
38.6
21.6



The fair yearly fee for the guarantee alone is about 0.79%. A weekly delta hedge removed about 95% of the risk, and the hedge error shrinks as rebalancing becomes more frequent. The reserve is far above the price because they answer different questions: the price is a risk-neutral value, and the reserve is capital for a bad market.



Hedge error at year 10 for monthly, weekly and daily rebalancing

title: Options Pricing Engine
text:
Limitations and assumptions

Most seg fund inputs are assumptions, not data: volatility, expected return and lapse rate. The results move a lot with them. One point of interest rate moves the cost of the guarantee by about 25% to 30%.
Black-Scholes is a formula for European options, and Tesla’s options are American. I did not measure the difference.
Volatility is a single constant in the models, while real options show a smile.
In the seg fund model, lapses are independent of the market and the pool of policies is large. Both are assumptions, and both probably understate the cost.
The CTE reserve illustrates a tail measure. It is not the regulatory formula.
Market data comes from Yahoo Finance and can lag by a day. The Shiny app runs locally in RStudio and is not published online.

title: Options Pricing Engine
text:
What I learned

Passing tests can still hide bugs. An Asian option with one monitoring step must equal the plain call, and it did not, because R had flattened a one-column matrix. The ordinary tests had passed.
A wrong sign can look plausible. My barrier correction moved the barrier the wrong way and gave 8.42, while the exact formula gave 7.587 and the corrected simulation matched it.
Real data is messy, and parity checks help. They exposed a mismatch between the stock price and the price the options were quoted at.
Assumptions drive the answer. The honest way to present a result like the guarantee’s cost is to show how much it moves with each input.
